citation: Zhang Q, Duan Z, Xiang D, Yu Y, Tian J. The effects of prosocial cartoon examples on children's donating behavior. Psychology Research and Behavior Management 14:1257-1268
experiment: Single experiment (2 cartoon x 2 gender x 3 age between-subjects design, pretest-posttest)
arm_label: Prosocial (charitable donation) cartoons vs control cartoons
treatment_description: Four Peppa Pig and related cartoon episodes in which characters donate or raise money for charity (e.g. running to raise money, giving toys to children in a mountain area, blood donation); 15 min per day on 4 consecutive days, watched in groups of about 13.
control_description: Four episodes of the same franchise with no donation content (talent day, perfume-making, train trip, fishing); paper: 'control cartoons did not include any donation contents and scenes' (p. 1260).
outcome_description: Toy Donation Task: number of 5 identical teddy bears (0-5) donated to disadvantaged peers via the China Hope Project; bears not donated were kept.
quote: Table 4, row Cartoon: Mean Square "68.01"; F(df1, df2) "60.22*** (1,144)"; ηp² "0.28"
location: Table 4, p. 1263 (ns from Table 1, p. 1259 and Table 3, p. 1263)
notes: F is the cartoon main effect from a 2 (cartoon) x 2 (gender) x 3 (age) ANOVA with no covariate (p. 1262), df2 = 144. The paper does not label the dependent variable as posttest, but Table 3 means (about 4.3 prosocial, about 3.0 control) differ from pretest Table 2 (2.29 vs 2.56), so Tables 3-4 are posttest. No pooled posttest mean per condition is reported; Table 3 gives by gender: prosocial male 4.28±0.83, female 4.38±0.78; control male 3.23±1.39, female 2.79±1.28 (39 children per cell; 78 per condition). Pretest (Table 2): prosocial 2.29±1.30, control 2.56±1.41; pretest t(154) = -1.24, p = 0.22. Children kept the bears they did not donate, so giving was costly; actual delivery of donated bears to the China Hope Project is not documented. Randomization: 'Half of them were randomly assigned to watch prosocial cartoons' (p. 1260), procedure otherwise not detailed. No preregistration statement in the text; data at osf.io/ae78r. primary_outcome true because donation is the study's only outcome.

citation: Chen H, Lyu D, Zhu L. The effectiveness of social-themed picture book reading in promoting children's prosocial behavior. Frontiers in Psychology 16
experiment: Single experiment (parent-child shared reading intervention, pretest-posttest)
arm_label: Social-themed picture books vs non-social picture books (sharing outcome)
country: China (one kindergarten in a southwestern city)
treatment_description: Parent-child reading of 16 social-themed picture books (cooperation 3, sharing 5, helping 4, friendship 4), twice a week for 8 weeks, 20-30 min per session.
control_description: Parent-child reading of 16 books on science, creativity and daily habits, matched on length, illustration-to-text ratio and interactive format, without social-emotional content.
delay: unclear: posttest given 'after the intervention ended' (8-week programme); interval from the last reading not reported
outcome_description: Sharing task adapted from a dictator game: number of the child's 7 chosen stickers placed, unobserved, in an envelope for children at another kindergarten.
quote: Table 3, Sharing row, posttest: intervention group "1.04 (1.18)"; control group "0.93 (1.53)". Table 1: "Intervention group (n = 30)", "Control group (n = 30)"
location: Results, 'Descriptive statistics', Table 3 (posttest columns); ns from Table 1
notes: Table 3 caption says 'Means and standard errors', but the values in parentheses match the SDs given in Table 1 and the text, and SEs would imply implausible SDs on a 0-7 scale; recorded as means_sd. Check. Pretest sharing: intervention 0.50 (1.00), control 0.90 (1.39), so groups were unbalanced at baseline. No attrition reported ('the 60 children' followed up), but the reported group x time interaction for total prosocial behaviour has df = 55 (F = 4.633, p = 0.036, eta² = 0.077); that test combines sharing with the pen-drop helping task (H stratum) and was not extracted. No separate test for sharing. Helping (pen-drop, H stratum) and parent-rated empathy (EmQue) not extracted. Assignment: 'Parent–child dyads were assigned at random', method not described. Whether shared stickers were actually delivered is not stated. primary_outcome false because the authors name no primary outcome and analyse only the combined total score. No preregistration statement; only a G*Power analysis.

citation: Ferro J, Guerra J-A. Making inequality unacceptable: an experiment on fiction reading and prosociality. AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0015996; presented at Seminario CEDE, Universidad de los Andes (unpublished)
notes: No paper or results available. AEA registry AEARCTR-0015996 opened: status 'On going', end date 2026-11-30; individual computer randomization to a 4-6 week fiction reading course vs a behavioural economics course; outcomes include dictator, ultimatum, trust and third-party games at course end and 4 weeks later; pilot 60 students, 'effective number of participants' N = 227; no results posted. Fiction texts not named, so cooperative content not verified. Seminario CEDE page (30 April 2026) abstract reports qualitatively that the fiction course increased prosocial behaviour, 'primarily through higher altruism and greater trustworthiness', with no numbers and no linked paper.

citation: Sakai JT, Chintaluru Y, Raymond KM, McWilliams S, Carter RM, Winters DE, Mikulich-Gilbertson SK. A revised prosocial behavior game: testing associations with psychopathic traits and the effects of moral elevation using a randomized clinical trial. PLOS ONE 18(4):e0283279
experiment: Single randomized trial (Run 1 game, video, Run 2 game)
arm_label: Moral elevation video vs nature control video
treatment_description: Moral elevation video that 'depicts a man risking his life to save another in the New York subway' (rescue, self-sacrifice).
control_description: 'a control nature video of similar length': images of the ocean, green spaces and forests.
outcome_description: AlAn's Short Game v.2: number of prosocial choices (Active Type A trials rejected, where accepting gains the subject money and lowers a Red Cross donation; Type B trials accepted, where the subject loses money and the Red Cross donation rises); Run 2 vs Run 1.
quote: The Group by Run interaction was non-significant (F1, 478 = 2.40; p = 0.122)
location: Results (section 3); arm ns from Fig 4 caption (moral elevation n = 237; control n = 248)
notes: F is the Group x Run (pre/post video) interaction, i.e. the difference in change between groups; it is unsigned and the text gives no direction ('relatively stable levels of prosocial behavior across runs 1 and 2'). Fig 4 shows adjusted estimates with SEs, not readable as text. Group main effect F1,478 = 0.42, p = 0.52 (averages pre- and post-video runs). df 478 with n = 485 analysed (modified ITT of 500 recruited) suggests covariates; not explained. 'Subjects were paid $20 plus earnings from playing the AlAn's Short Game v.2', so own-payoff stakes were real; whether Red Cross donations were actually paid is not stated. Video depicts a real event (modern, not invented); coded modern_invented as the nearest category. Target coded stranger (charity). Group numbering differs between Methods (Group 1 = elevation) and Results (Group 1 = control). Registered NCT03834467. primary_outcome true: not labelled primary, but it is the only outcome for the elevation test.

citation: Smith KM, Mabulla IA, Apicella CL. Hearing prosocial stories increases Hadza hunter-gatherers' generosity in an economic game. Human Nature 34(1):103-121
notes: Springer page shows abstract only; WSU Research Exchange record has no file; PMC returned a captcha page; OSF API request (api.osf.io/v2/nodes/rpbmz/files/osfstorage/) timed out awaiting permission and was not retried or routed around. Per-condition ns and assignment not available.

citation: Horton JJ, Rand DG, Zeckhauser RJ. The online laboratory: conducting experiments in a real labor market. Experimental Economics 14:399-425 (religious priming replication experiment)
experiment: Section 3.4 'Replication: Priming' (one of several experiments in the paper)
arm_label: Religious passage (Mark 10:17-23) vs neutral passage (fish species)
country: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers; country of residence used as a control but composition not reported
treatment_description: Read 'a Christian religious passage about the importance of charity (Mark 10:17-23)' before the game.
control_description: Read 'a passage of equal length describing three species of fish.'
outcome_description: One-shot prisoner's dilemma with another MTurk worker, cooperate = 1, defect = 0; payoffs in cents (CC 120/120, CD 40/160, DC 160/40, DD 80/80) plus $0.20 show-up fee, paid individually.

values.other: Logistic regression with robust SEs on PD cooperation: main effect of prime p = 0.169 (coefficient not reported); believer p = 0.12; prime x believer interaction coeff = 2.15, p = 0.001; gender coeff = 0.70, p = 0.044. n religious prime = 90, n neutral = 99. No cooperation rates by condition reported in the text; cell values appear only in Figure 1.

quote: no significant main effect of prime (p=0.169) or believer (p=0.12), but a significant positive interaction between the two (coeff= 2.15, p=0.001)
location: Section 3.4 and Figure 1, arXiv:1004.2931 (arXiv text has no page numbers; published Experimental Economics 14:399-425)
notes: Sample sizes quote: 'the religious prime group (N = 90) or a neutral prime group (N = 99)'. The prime main-effect p appears to come from the model that also includes the prime x believer interaction, so it is not a simple overall treatment vs control test. Figure 1 ('Reading a religious passage significantly increases prisoner's dilemma cooperation among those who believe in God but not among non-believers') holds the cooperation rates by condition and belief; it is an image and could not be read through the text-only fetch tool, so no numbers were taken from it. Number of believers vs non-believers not reported. weird left null: MTurk pool, country composition not reported (the paper discusses both US and India workers). Mark 10:17-23 is a narrative passage (rich young man told to give to the poor). No preregistration mentioned.

citation: Decety J, Cowell JM, Dajani R. Reading about people's feelings increases empathic concern and generosity in children (manuscript, Harvard scholar page)
experiment: Single experiment, Amman sample (pre/post, intervention vs control)
arm_label: Emotional reading intervention vs control group
treatment_description: 'emotional reading intervention': children 'were read stories about people's interactions and feelings' (Figure 1 caption); number, duration and frequency of sessions not reported.
control_description: Not described; text says only 'These changes were not present in the control group.' Possibly a no-text control (flag).
delay: unclear: interval between intervention and post-test not reported
outcome_description: Child-modified dictator game: number of stickers shared (Figure 1 axis 0-5); recipient and number of stickers available not stated.
quote: reveal a trending interaction effect of time x group (F (1, 42) = 3.69, p =.06, partial η2= .081)
location: p. 2 (ns: intervention n = 26, control n = 19, pp. 1-2)
notes: F is the time (pre/post) x group interaction from a 2x2 repeated-measures ANOVA, i.e. difference in change; df2 = 42 implies 44 analysed vs 45 enrolled (26 + 19), not explained. Within-group paired tests: intervention t(24) = -2.89, p < .01 (df inconsistent with n = 26); control t(18) = -.161, ns. Means and SDs not reported in text; Figure 1 shows pre/post bars with SE bars but no printed values (image not read). Abstract: generosity rose 'by nearly 100%'. Cooperative content of the stories not verified (emotion-focused stories about people's interactions and feelings); story source unknown, coded modern_invented as nearest category. Control activity not described (protocol flag: possible no-text control). incentivized coded true because stickers were shared in a dictator game, but stakes and recipient are not described. Random assignment stated: 'Prior to random assignment to intervention or control group' (p. 2). Year and publication status unknown; file name suggests 2015. primary_outcome false: no primary outcome designated; empathic concern and generosity are both headline outcomes. No preregistration mentioned.
